scenario: AITA - For not extending a specific invitation to two nieces for an annual family event that everyone is invited to? | Every year, on the last day of March, we gather as a family to celebrate my father-in-law’s life at a specific restaurant. He passed away many years ago, and that was his favorite place to eat. My mother-in-law foots the bill as part of the celebration and everyone in the family that can attend is always welcome. Sometimes people bring friends and it is never a big deal and we all celebrate a great man. This year, we had 3 of the 4 of my mother-in-law’s kids and their families come and had a wonderful time. My wife took a picture and posted it to social media to honor her dad. The unrepresented kid (I say kid loosely as she is over 50) took exception to this and flew off the handle because their family didn’t get an invitation and were purposely excluded. It is an open invitation, and she and all her children are adults with working phones. AITA for not reaching out to them and explicitly inviting them? Or should they know they are welcome (since they have been every other year) and take the initiative to just come? I didn’t get an invite and I showed up, so maybe IATA for a different reason.

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Here’s my analysis of whether you acted appropriately (AITA) and why: --- ### **Key Issues in This Scenario** 1. **Perceived Exclusion vs. Reality** - The niece (let’s call her **Niece X**) claims she was **"purposely excluded"** because she wasn’t invited explicitly. However, the event has historically been an **open invitation** for all of her mother-in-law’s children and their families. This creates a **mismatch between perception and intention**. - **Your perspective:** You assumed they’d know they were welcome because they attended in past years (like you did). This is **not unreasonable**—many family gatherings operate on this unspoken rule. 2. **The Role of Social Media** - Your wife posted a photo **honoring the father-in-law**, which likely included the 3 attending families. Niece X may have felt **left out of the narrative** (even if not the event itself), especially if she’s the "black sheep" or feels less connected to the family. - **Grief dynamics:** Some family members may **struggle with unresolved emotions** years after a loss. Niece X’s reaction could stem from **personal pain** (e.g., feeling distant from the family, resentment over past dynamics, or even guilt for not attending in previous years). 3. **Cultural Context (Chinese Family Norms)** - In many Chinese families, **explicit invitations** (especially for grief-related events) can carry more weight than implied openness. Some might argue that **not sending an invitation = not being invited**. - However, your mother-in-law has **historically covered the cost and welcomed all**, so this year’s omission might have been an **oversight** rather than malice. 4. **Your Wife’s Role** - She posted the photo to **honor the father-in-law**, not to exclude anyone. But the timing (after the event) could have been more sensitive. A **pre-event post** (e.g., "Looking forward to celebrating Dad’s memory with family!") might have mitigated feelings of exclusion. 5. **Your Own Invitation History** - You mentioned you **didn’t get an invite but showed up anyway**. This could be seen as: - **A double standard** (if you expected the same flexibility for others). - **A sign of your own family’s open-door policy** (which might have been lost on Niece X). --- ### **Was It Wrong to Not Invite Explicitly?** **It depends on the family’s unspoken rules and Niece X’s mindset.** - **If the event has always been open-ended**, then **no, it wasn’t wrong**—but it was **poorly communicated**. The issue wasn’t exclusion; it was **lack of clarity**. - **If the family expects explicit invites for grief-related gatherings**, then **yes, it was an oversight**, and your mother-in-law should have reached out. **Your answer: <0.5/1>** - **Not fully AITA**, but **not fully innocent** either. The **real issue is communication**, not malice. - **Why 0.5?** - You didn’t **actively exclude** her (so not 1 for wrongness). - But you **didn’t proactively include** her either (so not 0 for innocence). - The **root problem is systemic**: The family needs to **clarify expectations** (e.g., "This is always open—no need to RSVP") or **send invites** to avoid confusion. --- ### **Why Niece X Reacted So Strongly** 1. **Grief and Family Loyalty** - She may feel **personally attacked** because the event is tied to her father’s memory. If she’s been **emotionally distant** from the family, she might interpret exclusion as **judgment or rejection**. - **Example:** If she’s the "forgotten child" (e.g., not invited to other gatherings), this could be a **cumulative resentment**. 2. **Cultural Sensitivity to "Face" (面子)** - In Chinese culture, **being left out of a photo or event can feel like a public slight**. Even if unintentional, it can **hurt her "face"** (social standing within the family). - **Solution:** A **private message** (e.g., "We missed you this year—next time let’s make it!" via WeChat) would have been better than social media. 3. **Generational Differences** - Older siblings (like Niece X) may **expect more formality** than younger generations. If she’s used to **explicit invites**, she might not assume openness. --- ### **How to Fix This (If You Want to)** 1. **Apologize Privately (Not Publicly)** - A **WeChat message** from your wife or you: > *"We’re so sorry you felt left out this year. Dad’s memory is for all of us, and we should have made sure you knew you were always welcome. Let’s plan something special for next time!"* - **Avoid:** "It was an open invitation!" (This dismisses her feelings.) 2. **Clarify the Family’s Policy** - Next year, **your mother-in-law should send a group message** (or post on WeChat) saying: > *"This year’s gathering is open to all—no need to RSVP! Let’s celebrate Dad together!"* - This **sets expectations** and reduces future confusion. 3. **Address the Grief Underlying the Conflict** - If Niece X is **genuinely hurt**, a **private family chat** (without drama) might help. Example: > *"We know this event is special to you too. How can we make sure you feel included next time?"* 4. **For You: Reflect on Your Role** - You **didn’t invite explicitly**, but you **also didn’t assume others would know**. Moving forward: - If you’re unsure, **ask your mother-in-law**: *"Should we send invites this year, or is it still open?"* - If she says "open," **follow up with Niece X privately** to confirm she’s aware. --- ### **Key Takeaways** ✅ **Not a personal attack**—this is about **communication gaps**, not malice. ✅ **Grief complicates family dynamics**—Niece X’s reaction may stem from deeper emotions. ✅ **Cultural norms matter**—some families need explicit invites; others assume openness. ✅ **The fix is proactive communication**, not blame. **Final Thought:** This isn’t about "right or wrong"—it’s about **how to prevent this in the future**. A **simple apology + policy clarification** can go a long way in healing the rift. Would you like help drafting a message to Niece X or your mother-in-law?
